answer.label: Not Thomas Edison — an unsourced attribution
answer.authorDates: Credited to Thomas Edison (1847–1931) · earliest located printing: January 1981
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this two-sentence line under Disputed: the earliest appearance anyone has located is The A-V Magazine Vol. 89, No. 1 (January 1981), p. 18 — almost half a century after Edison died in 1931 — with a second printing in Jon Wynne-Tyson’s The Extended Circle (1985). The citation that usually travels with it, “Harper’s Magazine (1890),” has never been substantiated: Wikiquote records that no occurrence prior to the 1981 appearance has been located ↗.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — endlessly reprinted, but no printing has been found in Edison’s lifetime.

source.excerpt: Non-violence leads to the highest ethics, which is the goal of all evolution. Until we stop harming all other living beings, we are still savages.
trail: Wikiquote places the line in its Disputed section for Thomas Edison ↗, citing The A-V Magazine Vol. 89, No. 1 (January 1981), p. 18 and The Extended Circle (1985), p. 75, and noting that the widely repeated “Harper’s Magazine (1890)” citation has no located occurrence prior to 1981.
The 1981 magazine is the quarterly of the American Anti-Vivisection Society ↗ — an advocacy publication, not an Edison archive, and no primary Edison document is named alongside it.
The second printing is Jon Wynne-Tyson’s The Extended Circle: A Dictionary of Humane Thought (Fontwell: Centaur, 1985) ↗, a widely used anthology that lent the attribution a reference-book veneer.

Full-text search across the Internet Archive’s scanned books ↗ returns the sentence only in modern books — vegan, animal-welfare and quotation titles predominate — and nothing predates 1981, consistent with a line that entered print in the 1980s.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller original context to show, because no original has been found. This is the complete two-sentence form as Wikiquote records it under Disputed ↗; the first sentence often circulates alone.
source.rightsNote: No status is asserted here. The wording cannot be tied to any identified author or to a specific first publication — the earliest located printing is a January 1981 magazine, and whoever composed the sentence is unknown. Because the origin is unknown, this page makes no public-domain claim; anyone reproducing the line should treat its status as unresolved.

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.heading: About Thomas Edison
author.bio: Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman, born 11 February 1847 and dead on 18 October 1931 — the man behind the phonograph, the commercial incandescent lamp and the Menlo Park and West Orange research laboratories. Nothing in the documented record shows him writing or speaking about non-violence toward animals, and the best-known animal episode of his career runs the other way: during the war of the currents, Harold Brown electrocuted four calves and a lame horse with 750 volts of alternating current at Edison’s West Orange laboratory on 5 December 1888, with Edison looking on. The line quoted here is a modern arrival that borrows his name, not a sentiment he is known to have expressed.

misattribution.heading: How this became an Edison quote
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook name-magnet quote: a clean, quotable moral claim with a famous name bolted on and a plausible-sounding citation that dissolves the moment you check it.

items.why: Wikiquote lists it under Disputed ↗ and states that no occurrence has been located prior to a January 1981 printing — long after Edison’s death on 18 October 1931. No letter, notebook, interview or published article of his has been produced.
The quote is frequently reprinted with this source. Wikiquote records the citation and flags that no occurrence prior to 1981 has been located ↗ — so the 1890 reference is repeated, not demonstrated.

Jon Wynne-Tyson’s dictionary of humane thought ↗ printed the line on p. 75 and gave it the authority of a reference book, but it post-dates the 1981 magazine appearance and is not an independent witness to Edison.
During the war of the currents, Harold Brown electrocuted four calves and a lame horse with alternating current at Edison’s West Orange laboratory on 5 December 1888, with Edison looking on ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody knows who wrote it. The oldest copy anyone has found is a January 1981 anti-vivisection magazine ↗, and until an earlier source surfaces the line should not be quoted as Edison’s.

context.heading: Why this one spread
lead: The sentence is built to travel. It opens with an abstraction almost nobody argues with (“non-violence leads to the highest ethics”), ties it to evolution — which sounds scientific — and closes with a one-word verdict on anyone who disagrees: savages. Bolt on the name of America’s most famous inventor and you have a line that reads as though a hard-headed man of science arrived at compassion by reasoning rather than sentiment.

Its documented life begins in the animal-advocacy press. The earliest printing anyone has located is the January 1981 issue of The A-V Magazine, the quarterly of the American Anti-Vivisection Society ↗; the second located printing is Jon Wynne-Tyson’s 1985 anthology The Extended Circle ↗, which gave the line reference-book standing. Search the Internet Archive’s book corpus today and the sentence surfaces only in modern books — vegan, animal-welfare and quotation titles predominate — with nothing predating 1981, let alone an Edison-era text.
context.detailsSummary: The awkward part: Edison and the animals
detailsBody: The quote asks readers to stop harming other living beings. Edison’s best-documented dealings with animals were the opposite. In the late-1880s war of the currents, electrical engineer Harold Brown set out to prove alternating current was lethal; he approached Edison, who offered assistance, and Brown was given space, equipment and a laboratory assistant at Edison’s West Orange laboratory.

On 5 December 1888, in that laboratory and with Edison looking on ↗, Brown killed four calves and a lame horse with 750 volts of AC. That does not by itself prove Edison could never have written the quoted sentence decades later — people change — but it is a reason to want a real source before putting these words in his mouth, and no real source exists.
context.pull: The oldest copy anyone can find is younger than the Walkman.
